p.x:
Every month, my friends and I join a beach clean-up near our town. It's free, and anyone can help. Last Saturday, about forty people came. The leader gave everyone a bag and gloves, and we worked together for three hours.
We collected plastic bottles, bags and even an old shoe! I had to carry two heavy bags to the truck. Some people brought water and fruit for everyone. At the end, we took a big photo together.
I love doing this at the weekend because I care about the sea. It's also a good way to meet new people. Last month, I became a member of the group, and now I help organise the events. Why don't you come next time?

Nok is a 22-year-old university student, but she spends most of her free time volunteering. Two years ago, she signed up to help at a food bank in her community. Every Saturday, she sorts donations of rice, oil and tinned food, and gives them to families who need them.
On Wednesday evenings, Nok visits a nursing home, where she plays games and chats with elderly people. "Many of them are lonely," she says. "Just listening to them makes a difference." She also works as a mentor for a teenager from an orphanage, helping him with his studies.
Last year, Nok organised a fundraising concert for a children's charity and raised 80,000 baht. "People were very generous," she remembers. "Everyone contributed something, even if it was only twenty baht."
Why does she do it? "It's very rewarding," she explains. "I've learned more from volunteering than from any classroom."

Volunteering is often described as an act of pure altruism: people giving their time without expecting anything in return. Yet research suggests that the motives are more complex, and that this is not necessarily a bad thing.
Many volunteers admit that they also benefit personally. They gain skills, make friends and feel a sense of purpose. Studies have even linked regular volunteering to lower stress and longer life. In this sense, volunteers are themselves beneficiaries of the work they do.
Volunteering also plays a wider role in society. Grassroots groups, from neighbourhood clean-ups to youth clubs, strengthen social cohesion by bringing together people who might otherwise never meet. Nonprofit organisations often reach marginalised communities that government outreach programmes fail to serve. By participating, citizens develop a stronger sense of civic responsibility.
Critics, however, warn that volunteers should not replace properly funded public services. When governments cut welfare budgets and expect charities to fill the gaps, the burden falls on generous individuals rather than on society as a whole. The ideal, many argue, is a partnership: the state guarantees basic rights, while volunteers add warmth, solidarity and local knowledge, empowering communities to help themselves. Those who dedicate their time can then focus on making life better rather than simply surviving, and any petition for change carries more weight when it comes from an active community.
